title: L.O.L.: Lack of Love
subtitle: Life on a changing planet
summary: L.O.L.: Lack of Love is Love-de-Lic's life simulation, first released for Dreamcast in Japan on 2 November 2000.
body: L.O.L.: Lack of Love is Love-de-Lic's life simulation, first released for Dreamcast in Japan on 2 November 2000. The player controls a creature on an alien planet being transformed by machines. Staying alive involves finding relationships with other life forms and adapting to the changing environment. Director Kenichi Nishi and composer Ryuichi Sakamoto developed the project around ideas associated with the Gaia hypothesis, which considers the interactions between life and its surroundings. The game presents those concerns through the creature's immediate needs and encounters rather than a conventional sequence of missions.

Communicating with other creatures and helping them establishes symbiotic relationships that allow the protagonist to change form. Food, sleep and other bodily needs also shape survival, with very little conventional interface separating the player from the environment. Progress comes from observing what another creature is doing and finding a useful way to respond. An encounter may provide help or sustenance, but it also belongs to a larger network of living things. Learning that network changes what the small protagonist can become and where it can continue to survive.

Sakamoto's music supports the unfamiliar landscape while the lack of a prominent display leaves attention on behaviour and surroundings. The project followed Moon and UFO in Love-de-Lic's short history, sharing an interest in actions outside conventional combat and conquest. Its Japanese-only commercial release limited the original audience, with a fan translation arriving much later. The central idea remains direct in play: the creature develops through contact with others, making care, observation and dependence into the means of moving through a world whose future is being altered around it.
